data.claim: A multi-line quoted string stops _split from treating ; as a command separator, so commands after the ; are never matched.
data.falsifier: check('echo a; git push origin main; python3 -c "<newline>print(1)"') returns a Refusal naming git push instead of None.
data.mechanism: _split tokenizes each physical line separately. A quote spanning a newline makes shlex raise ValueError on the line that opens it, so the line.split() fallback is used, which leaves ; glued to the preceding word (-q;, main;), and the after-; commands are swallowed into the first command.

data.question: Does the forbidden-command guard miss commands after a semicolon when the line holds a multi-line quoted string?

chunk_findings.detail: `_strip_continuations` treats every `'` as a single-quoted span and, if the closer is missing, stops stripping backslash-newlines for the rest of the text. A `'` inside double quotes is literal in bash, so `echo "it's $\` + newline + `(git push origin main)"` (and `echo "'$\` + newline + `(git push origin main)"`) still joins to `$(git push origin main)` and runs it. After the stripper leaves the `\`-newline in place, `dquote` sees `$` then `\` and skips the newline instead of a `(`, so `_substitutions` never records `git push` and `_check` returns None. The regression strings have no `'` before the continuation, so they do not catch this.

chunk_findings.detail: `command` sets `cut` on every newline in a `$(...)` or backtick body, and `_logical_lines` uses that same array to split the outer script. Those newlines separate only the inner command. For `echo "$(echo x\n)"; git push origin main`, bash runs `git push`, but the cut breaks the outer line into `echo "$(echo x` and `)"; git push origin main`. `shlex` (posix, the second line) treats the leading `"` as an unclosed quote and swallows `; git push origin main` as data, and the substitution body is only `echo x\n`, so `_check` returns None. The same split happens for any forbidden command after `;` following a double-quoted substitution that contains a newline.

chunk_findings.detail: `_strip_continuations` treats every `'` as a quote delimiter and never a backslash-escaped literal, so a `\<newline>` that bash still removes (line continuation is decided only for an unquoted backslash) is left in the text. `_scan` then skips that pair as an ordinary escape and never sees `$` adjacent to `(`. chunk_findings.detail: `find_body` lost the old `elif c == "\\":` skip, so a backslash-escaped closer is treated as the end of the command substitution. For example, in `echo $(echo \)\n); git push origin main` (the `)` after `\` is escaped, and the following newline is inside the real `$()` body), `if c == closer: return k` returns the escaped `)`, not the real closing `)`. This is exactly the “newline inside `$()` is split out of the outer line” failure this change is meant to prevent, and it can make the matcher inspect the wrong fragment instead of the actual command. chunk_findings.detail:
`_scan` does not account for shell comments, where quote characters have no effect. Given the command string:
```
echo hi # don't
git push 'origin main'
```
Bash ignores `don't` as a comment and then runs `git push 'origin main'`, which the forbidden-command guard must refuse. But `_scan` sees the `'` in `don't` as an opening single quote; `text.find("'", i + 1)` finds the `'` of `'origin main'` on the next line and jumps past it, so the separating newline is never marked in `cut`. `_logical_lines` returns the two physical lines as one merged line. `_split` then passes that merged string to `shlex` with `lex.commenters = ""`, and `git` is absorbed into the single-quoted span opened by the comment apostrophe, so `git` is not a starting command token. `F.check` returns None for this actual forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_scan single-quote branch

chunk_findings.detail: `find_body` treats the first `)` or backtick as the closer and never skips a backslash escape, unlike the top-level `_scan` loop. Bash does not close `$(...)` on `\)` and does not end an old-style substitution on `\``. Given `echo "$(echo \); git push origin main)"`, the inner shell runs `git push`, but `find_body` stops at `\)`, so the recorded body is only `echo \` and the `; git push origin main` left behind stays inside the double quotes. `_split` therefore never sees `git` as a command, and the same miss happens for `` echo "`echo \`; git push origin main`" ``. The guard returns no hit.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_find_body` only understands plain `'...'` quotes, not bash ANSI-C quotes (`$'...'`). In `$'a\')'`, the `\'` is an escaped literal quote and the following `)` is still inside the ANSI-C-quoted word, so it does **not** close an enclosing `$(...)`. But the `if c == "'":` branch calls `text.find("'", k + 1)` and takes the escaped `'` as the end of the quote, so the next character `)` is returned as the substitution close. Given
`echo $(echo $'a\')' ; git push origin main ; echo done)`
bash runs `git push origin main` inside the `$(...)` body, but the scanner stores only `echo $'a\'` as the body and stops there; `git push origin main` is never added to a scanned line or body. The same bypass applies to any source that uses `$'...'` with an escaped quote before a literal `)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `#`-comment test `(i == 0 or text[i - 1] in " \t\r\n;|&()<>")` treats a `#` as a comment after any single `)`, but the `)` that closes a `$(...)` substitution is part of the same shell word, not a word boundary. Given
`echo $(echo hi)#bar"<NL>"; git push origin main`
where `<NL>` is a literal newline, bash treats `#` literally (`echo $(echo hi)#bar` prints `hi#bar`), and the double quote spans the newline, so the semicolon really runs `git push origin main`. This guard instead skips from `#` to `<NL>`, cuts there, and passes the second chunk `"; git push origin main` to shlex; that leading `"` is unclosed in the chunk and swallows `; git push origin main` as data, so `F.check` misses the forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:215

chunk_findings.detail: The new comment skip treats `#` as a comment whenever the previous character is in `<>`, but bash only starts a comment at the beginning of a word. After a redirection operator the next token is a filename, so `>#` / `<#` is literal. Given `echo ok >#x; git push origin main` (also `echo ok <#x; git push origin main` and `echo ok &>#x; git push origin main`), bash runs `git push` after the redirection to a file named `#x...`, while `_scan` jumps from that `#` to EOL and never sees the command, so the guard returns None. A space before `#` (`echo ok > #x; git push ...`) is a real comment and is not this case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:215

chunk_findings.detail:
`_scan` does not account for shell comments, where quote characters have no effect. Given the command string:
```
echo hi # don't
git push 'origin main'
```
Bash ignores `don't` as a comment and then runs `git push 'origin main'`, which the forbidden-command guard must refuse. But `_scan` sees the `'` in `don't` as an opening single quote; `text.find("'", i + 1)` finds the `'` of `'origin main'` on the next line and jumps past it, so the separating newline is never marked in `cut`. `_logical_lines` returns the two physical lines as one merged line. `_split` then passes that merged string to `shlex` with `lex.commenters = ""`, and `git` is absorbed into the single-quoted span opened by the comment apostrophe, so `git` is not a starting command token. `F.check` returns None for this actual forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_scan single-quote branch

chunk_findings.detail: `find_body` treats the first `)` or backtick as the closer and never skips a backslash escape, unlike the top-level `_scan` loop. Bash does not close `$(...)` on `\)` and does not end an old-style substitution on `\``. Given `echo "$(echo \); git push origin main)"`, the inner shell runs `git push`, but `find_body` stops at `\)`, so the recorded body is only `echo \` and the `; git push origin main` left behind stays inside the double quotes. `_split` therefore never sees `git` as a command, and the same miss happens for `` echo "`echo \`; git push origin main`" ``. The guard returns no hit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:161

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_find_body` returns at the first unescaped `)` for `$(` bodies, but valid shell has `)` tokens that do not close a command substitution. For example, in `echo $(case x in x) git push origin main;; esac); echo done`, Bash runs `git push origin main` as the `case` action, so the forbidden-command guard must refuse it. `_find_body` treats the `)` after `case x in x` as the substitution closer, so the recorded body is only `case x in x`; the leaked `git push ...` is glued onto the outer `echo` command with no separator before it and is not seen as the start of any command, so F.check misses it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail: `elif c == "#" and (i == 0 or text[i - 1] in " \t\r\n;|&()<>"):` treats any `#` after a `)` as the start of a comment. A `)` that closes `$()` is not a word boundary: in `echo $(echo x)#; git push origin main`, bash treats `$(echo x)#` as one word (expanding to the argument `x#`), so the `;` is a command separator and `git push origin main` is executed. `_scan` has already consumed the `$()` through `_find_body`, lands on `#`, enters the comment branch because the previous character is `)`, and skips the rest of the line; the forbidden command after `;` is never seen by `F.check`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_scan comment detection

chunk_findings.detail: `_find_body` still treats the first unquoted `)` / backtick as the end of a substitution and never skips a `#` comment, unlike the new top-level `#` branch in `_scan`. Inside `$(...)` a `#` that begins a word comments out the rest of that line, so a `)` there does not close the substitution. Given `echo "$(echo # )\ngit push origin main)"`, bash runs `git push` in the subshell (the `)` after `#` is comment text; the real closer is the `)` before the final `"`). `_find_body` returns at that commented `)`, records only `echo # `, and `_dquote_end` then keeps `git push origin main` inside the outer double quotes, so the guard never sees it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body
